fuller.text: This is a long essay by Paul Graham, written in July 2023, on how to do great work in any field. He imagined collecting lists of techniques from many fields and asked what they share, then wrote that shared core down. His claim is that the overlap has a definite shape, not just a single point labelled "work hard." The advice assumes the reader is very ambitious.

fuller.text: Graham says many more people could try to do great work than actually do. Modesty and fear hold them back, usually without a conscious decision: trying to be Newton seems presumptuous and likely to fail. He adds that smart, ambitious people who don't achieve much tend to become bitter.

fuller.text: The core is four steps, which he says nearly everyone who did great work followed, from painters to physicists. Choose a field you have a natural talent for, a deep interest in, and room to do great work. Learn enough to reach a frontier, the edge of what anyone knows. Notice the gaps there, which look smooth from far away but turn out to be everywhere up close. Explore the promising gaps.

fuller.text: Choosing what to work on is the hard part, because you can't tell what most work is like except by doing it. Biographies show how much luck is involved, so he says to make yourself a big target for luck by being curious. Rather than planning far ahead, he suggests "staying upwind": at each stage doing what seems most interesting and keeps your best options open.

fuller.text: On the work itself, consistency beats bursts: a page a day becomes a book a year. The most dangerous delay is putting off an ambitious project for years, which hides itself as being busy with other work. Setbacks are normal: great work is a search where you sometimes back up and try another path, but never drop the wish to do great work.

fuller.text: New ideas seem obvious afterward because finding them means fixing a broken model, a mistaken way of seeing the world. That takes being stricter than others about clues that don't fit, plus a willingness to break rules the old model takes for granted. He argues the real insight often lies in the question, not the answer.

fuller.text: The essay argues from experience and historical examples, not measurements, and it names its limits. Graham says great work has no precise definition or threshold; importance is a matter of degree and hard to judge at the time. He can't prove hard work is needed, though he calls the evidence as strong as the evidence that we die. He also doesn't know whether originality can be grown, only how to make the most of it.

fuller.text: If the secret had to be one word, his bet is "curiosity." He lists ability, interest, effort and luck as the factors, so the question becomes finding work where your ability and interest combine. He is optimistic that a close match probably exists for you, and says only trying will show how far it takes you.

brief.text: This essay by Paul Graham is a guide to doing great work in any field. He looked for the advice that many different fields share. He found it has a clear shape, not just "work hard."

He found it has a clear shape, not just "work hard."

brief.text: He lays out four steps: pick a field, and learn it up to the frontier. The frontier is the edge of what anyone knows so far. Then notice the gaps there, and explore the promising ones. His main conclusion is that curiosity drives all four steps.
